Probabilistic Microplastics Risk Characterization: Central California Rivers

Scott Coffin, Ph.D. — California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)

June 24, 2026

1 1. Overview

This document presents an end-to-end, fully probabilistic environmental risk assessment (ERA) workflow for microplastics in freshwater surface water and sediment from four central California rivers (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, and San Lorenzo). The workflow proceeds through five steps:

  1. Raw particle data → power-law slope (α) via C-PSD — cumulative particle size distribution fitted using the two-step LOD detection algorithm of Segur et al. (2026).
  2. Monitoring concentrations → probabilistic rescaling — power-law integration converts measurements from a sampled size range to a target range, propagating slope uncertainty via Monte Carlo (Coffin et al. 2022).
  3. Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED) — nonparametric bootstrap of corrected site-level concentrations.
  4. Hazard threshold distribution — probabilistic species sensitivity distributions (pSSD++) using the PSSDplusplus R package and ToMEx 2.0 toxicity database.
  5. Risk characterization — Monte Carlo pairing of exposure and hazard distributions, expressed as risk quotient (RQ = Exposure/Hazard) and exceedance probability P(RQ > 1).

All custom R functions (fit_cpsd_segur_r, correction_factor, bootstrap_eed, mc2d_risk, etc.) live in R/mp_risk_utils.R and R/cpsd_plotting.R for reuse and eventual integration into PSSDplusplus. The Segur et al. (2026) LOD-detection algorithm is implemented directly in R/mp_risk_utils.R as pure R.

3 3. Load data

3.1 3.1 Raw particle-length observations

This data comes from microscopy/FTIR particle measurements (a table of individual particles).

# import river particle data (includes plastics and non-plastics)
raw_particles <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_comb.rds") |> 
  # filter to only QC-passing particles
  dplyr::filter(!material_class %in% c("mineral", "organic matter"), #filter non-plastic
                acc_analy_conf == "confident", # only use confident spectra
                bad_spectra) %>% #filter out bad spectra
  # extract the first 8-digit block from the ID
  mutate(date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"), date = ymd(date_raw), # convert YYYYMMDD → Date
         shape = case_when(aspect_ratio >= 3 ~ "fiber", # common definition of fiber - check!
                           aspect_ratio <= 3 ~ "fragment"),
         length_um = max_length_um,
         width_um = min_length_um
  )

# subset by matrix for downstream analysis
raw_particles_river <- raw_particles |> 
  filter(sample_type == "river water") #river water, ocean water, or beach sand are options

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles |> 
  filter(sample_type == "ocean water")

raw_particles_river |> 
  group_by(shape) |> 
  summarize(count = n(),
            mean_length = mean(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_length = min(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_length = max(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_length = sd(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_width = mean(width_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_width = min(width_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_width = max(width_um, na.rm = TRUE)
            )

3.1.1 3.1.1 Estimate particle volume

# ---- Thickness (height) factor from measured raw data ----
# Kooi et al. (2022) H = r * W, where r is median(W/L). 
ratio_tbl <- raw_particles_river |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1/aspect_ratio,
    # area-derived effective width (rectangle proxy); protects against noisy min_length
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),            # central estimate
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),    # conservative low
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),    # conservative high
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# quick sanity check: ratio table + summary of volumes
ratio_tbl
# ---- Volumes ----
# Ellipsoid (Kooi-compatible): V = (pi/6) * L * W * H  with H = r * W
# => V = (pi/6) * r * L * W^2
# Cylinder assumption for fibers: V = pi * (W/2)^2 * L

raw_particles_river <- raw_particles_river |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(# thickness in um (assume L/W = H/W)
    height_um = r_med * width_um) |> 

    mutate(# ellipsoid volume in um^3 (primary; Kooi-consistent)
      V_um3  = case_when(shape == "fragment" ~ (pi/6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
    # fiber cylinder sensitivity in um^3 (only meaningful for fibers)
                        shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um/2)^2 * length_um,
                        TRUE ~ NA_real_)
                        ) |> 
    # estimate particle mass based on volume and assumed density
    mutate(mass_ug = V_um3 * 1.1) # assume density of 1.1 g/cm^3 for plastics

# export CSV of cleaned up raw particles
write.csv(raw_particles_river, "data_output/Part_dets_cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)

raw_particles_river |>
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    V_um3_median = median(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    V_um3_mean = mean(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    V_um3_sd = sd(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_median = median(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_mean = mean(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_sd = sd(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

3.2 3.2 Monitoring concentration observations (site replicates)

Here we load monitoring replicate concentrations (particles/L) that were reported for limited size ranges (e.g., 300–5000 µm typical of net tows).

monitoring <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds") |> 
  filter(sample_type == "river water",
         material_simple == "plastic",
         sample_or_blank == "sample"
  ) %>% 
  mutate(# extract the first 8-digit block from the ID
    date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"),  
    # convert YYYYMMDD → Date
    date = ymd(date_raw),    
    # correct the specific sample date
    date = case_when(
      Client_ID_MSSupdate == "SRR20250303SS" ~ ymd("20250303"),
      TRUE ~ date
    ),
    sample_dets = case_when(Client_ID_MSSupdate %in% c("CRR20231207SS", "CRR20231207SD") ~ "lagoon",
                            Client_ID_MSSupdate %in% c("SRR20231207SS", "SRR20231207SD") ~ "lagoon"),
    # recode depth to subsurface
    sample_depth_general = recode(sample_depth_general,
                                  "depth" = "subsurface"),
    sample_depth_general = factor(
      sample_depth_general,
      levels = c("subsurface", "surface")
    ) 
  ) %>%
  rename(river = sample_location,
         C_measured_pL = extrap_conc_PPL) |> 
          # should adjust based on power law LLOD determined below
  mutate(Lmin_measured_um = 50, 
         Lmax_measured_um = 500,
         sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate)

head(monitoring)

4 4. Step 1 — Derive power-law alpha via C-PSD (binned cumulative PSD)

4.1 4.1 C-PSD fitting — Segur et al. (2026)

The C-PSD (cumulative particle size distribution) method fits N(≥L) vs L on a log-log scale using binned count data, removing the bin-width bias inherent in the classic BN-PSD approach (Segur et al. 2026). The algorithm is implemented in pure R in R/mp_risk_utils.R as fit_cpsd_segur_r().

Two-step LOD detection algorithm:

  1. Bin particle measurements; compute BN-PSD and C-PSD.
  2. Global OLS on all bins → normalised residuals; retain bins with positive residuals at or above the BN-PSD peak (Low_size ≥ L_max of the BN-PSD).
  3. Exhaustively test all contiguous sub-windows ≥ 3 bins; accept windows with R² ≥ 0.90.
  4. Select the longest accepted window (ties broken by R²) as the fitting range.
  5. OLS on log₁₀ N(≥L) ~ log₁₀ L_low; BN-PSD slope a = a_cpsd − 1.

4.2 4.2 Fit C-PSD to the raw particle data

4.2.1 4.2.1 Particle Length

# Pooled C-PSD fits across all river locations, bin_um = 5 µm
cpsd_fit_frag  <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "fragment"))
cpsd_fit_fiber <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "fiber"))
cpsd_fit_all   <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::pull(length_um),              bin_um = 5), list(shape = "all"))

The Segur et al. (2026) algorithm fitted power-law slopes of α_CPSD = -2.71 ± 0.04 for fragments (LOD 95 – 350 µm), α_CPSD = -1.69 ± 0.04 for fibers (LOD 175 – 480 µm), and α_CPSD = -1.93 ± 0.03 for all particles pooled (LOD 165 – 385 µm, R² = 0.989). The corresponding differential BN-PSD slopes (a = α_CPSD − 1) are -3.71 (fragment), -2.69 (fiber), and -2.93 (all). For comparison, Segur et al. (2026) report a mean BN-PSD slope of −2.66 ± 0.68 for fragments across ocean and atmosphere samples.

# Per-location fits (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San Lorenzo) — all particles pooled by site
locations <- sort(unique(raw_particles_river$sample_location))

cpsd_fits_by_loc <- lapply(setNames(locations, locations), function(loc) {
  dat <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc) |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
  c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(dat, bin_um = 5), list(shape = loc))
})

# Summary table: slope and LOD window by location
loc_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
  fo <- cpsd_fits_by_loc[[loc]]
  tibble::tibble(
    location     = loc,
    n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_river$sample_location == loc),
    a_cpsd       = round(fo$a_cpsd,   3),
    se_a_cpsd    = round(fo$se_a_cpsd, 3),
    a_psd        = round(fo$a_psd,    3),
    lod_low_um   = round(fo$lower_lod_used_um, 0),
    lod_high_um  = round(fo$upper_lod_um,       0),
    r2           = round(fo$r2,       3),
    n_bins       = fo$n_bins,
    fit_mode     = fo$fit_mode
  )
}))

knitr::kable(loc_summary, caption = "C-PSD length fits by river location (Segur 2026 algorithm)")

4.2.1.1 4.2.1.1 Plot C-PSD fits (model uncertainty)

plot_cpsd_multi() and MP_PALETTE are sourced from R/cpsd_plotting.R.

fits_by_shape <- list(fragment = cpsd_fit_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_fiber, all = cpsd_fit_all)
fits_by_shape <- fits_by_shape[names(MP_PALETTE)[names(MP_PALETTE) %in% names(fits_by_shape)]]

alpha_cpsh_plot <- plot_cpsd_multi(

4.2.1.2 4.2.1.2 Literature comparison of power-law size distribution slopes

The differential BN-PSD slope apsd = acpsd − 1 (equivalent to the negative power-law exponent α in Kooi & Koelmans 2019) characterizes how steeply particle abundance declines with increasing size. Steeper (more negative) apsd values indicate that small particles dominate the count distribution far more strongly than large ones. Comparing this slope across studies and analytical methods provides a critical cross-check on data quality and reveals how sampling methodology shapes the apparent size distribution.

Notation reconciliation. Different publications use different sign conventions. Zhao et al. (2026) and Kooi & Koelmans (2019) report the positive exponent α from the probability density function f(L) ∝ L−α; their α corresponds directly to |apsd| in our Segur notation. Wang et al. (2026) follow the same positive-α convention. Segur et al. (2026) report the negative C-PSD slope acpsd, from which apsd = acpsd − 1.

Power-law size distribution slopes: this study vs. recent literature. All values converted to the BN-PSD differential slope a_psd for comparability.
Source Convention Reported value Equivalent a_psd

This study — fibers (µFTIR, Segur LOD, 175–480 µm) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.692 -2.692
This study — all shapes (µFTIR, Segur LOD, 165–385 µm) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.926 -2.926
Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine/Meuse combined suspended solids (µFTIR) BN-PSD +α (positive) 3.650 -3.650
Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine Lobith samples (µFTIR, mean) BN-PSD +α (positive) 3.890 -3.890
Wang et al. 2026 — Meuse Eijsden samples (µFTIR, mean) BN-PSD +α (positive) 3.190 -3.190
Segur et al. 2026 — ocean reference (C-PSD) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.660 -2.660
Segur et al. 2026 — atmosphere reference (C-PSD) C-PSD a_cpsd (negative) -1.550 -2.550
Zhao et al. 2026 — global surface water meta-analysis (45 studies) BN-PSD +α (positive) 1.500 -1.500
Zhao et al. 2026 — mesh-adjusted global surface water BN-PSD +α (positive) 1.530 -1.530
Kooi & Koelmans 2019 — global freshwater/marine BN-PSD +α (positive) 1.600 -1.600

Key finding — consistency with µFTIR studies, divergence from net-trawl surveys. Our fragment apsd (-3.71) and all-shape apsd (-2.93) are within the range reported by Wang et al. (2026) for Dutch river suspended solids measured by µFTIR (−3.19 to −3.89, mean combined −3.65, SD 0.21). This agreement is not surprising: both datasets use particle-by-particle µFTIR counting on filtered samples. In contrast, our values are substantially steeper than the global surface water meta-analysis compiled by Zhao et al. (2026; mean α = 1.50, equivalent apsd = −1.50, SD 0.53) and the global averages reported by Kooi & Koelmans (2019; α ≈ 1.60). The Segur et al. (2026) reference slopes (ocean −1.66, atmosphere −1.55 in C-PSD notation, equivalent apsd ≈ −2.66 and −2.55) are intermediate.

The divergence from the Zhao/Kooi global averages likely reflects three interacting factors: (1) analytical resolution — µFTIR counting captures particles approaching ~20 µm, whereas most studies in the Zhao meta-analysis used net trawls or pump samples with mesh sizes ≥ 300 µm, systematically missing the numerically dominant small-particle fraction and producing an apparent shallower slope; (2) size range of fit — our Segur LOD algorithm fits the C-PSD over a restricted window (~100–330 µm for fragments) within which the distribution is inherently steeper than a global fit spanning three orders of magnitude; (3) environmental context — California coastal rivers may differ from open-ocean or mixed-environment global compilations.

Fiber vs. fragment. Fibers exhibit a notably shallower slope (apsd = -2.69) than fragments (apsd = -3.71). This is consistent with Zhao et al. (2026), who found that fibers have dramatically lower mesh capture efficiency (0.70% at 330 µm mesh; 37.6% at 20 µm mesh across a 10–5000 µm size range) compared to fragments (7.9% at 330 µm). While our µFTIR pump-and-filter approach avoids the coarsest mesh bias, filter capture of fine fibers (whose short axis — diameter ≤ 10 µm — can pass through a nominal 50 µm pore) may still be lower than for equidimensional fragments. A shallower measured fiber slope would result if fine fibers are under-retained, making observed fiber concentrations a minimum estimate. Users comparing fiber-specific concentrations across studies should be aware of this potential systematic bias.

Implications for data correction. Three recently published correction methodologies were evaluated for applicability to this workflow:

  1. Zhao et al. (2026) — Mesh selectivity correction: This physically-based model corrects for particle loss during mesh-based net trawling or pump filtration. It is not applied here because (a) our particle data derive from µFTIR analysis of membrane-filtered samples where the Segur LOD algorithm explicitly identifies and corrects for the analytical lower detection limit; (b) the Zhao model is calibrated for net trawls (mesh aperture as the primary parameter) rather than membrane filtration; and (c) our correction_factor() function already accounts for size-range sampling bias through power-law integration, which accomplishes the same conceptual goal. Applying the Zhao correction on top of the existing CF would risk double-counting the lower-size adjustment.

  2. Wang et al. (2026) — µFTIR objective and sieve effects: Wang et al. demonstrated that the 4× µFTIR objective captures only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to the 25× objective (predominantly because the 4× misses sub-50 µm particles). The sieve mesh size (20 µm vs. 5 µm) had minimal effect on size distribution or polymer composition. The present dataset was collected with an approximately 4× objective at 25 µm pixel size, giving a detection floor of ~50 µm. Critically, this floor is already reflected in L_meas_min = 50 µm, and the power-law CF extrapolates particle counts from this floor to 1 µm. The Wang et al. ×33 factor therefore does not apply here — it would double-count the sub-50 µm extrapolation already performed by the CF. A detailed analysis of this intersection and the residual uncertainty in the 50–100 µm marginal detection zone is presented in Section 10.2.

  3. Chen et al. (2026) — Count-to-mass conversion: Chen et al. developed a conditional fragmentation distribution (CFD, Weibull-based) model for converting particle counts to mass, outperforming the simple power-law (CPD) approach. This methodology is not applicable to the present count-based risk assessment workflow (exposure expressed as particles/L); it would be relevant only if mass-based exposure concentrations were required for comparison with mass-normalized ecotoxicological thresholds.

Summary. The Segur et al. (2026) LOD detection and power-law correction workflow, as implemented here, represents a sound and methodologically consistent approach for central California riverine monitoring data. The measured slopes are coherent with other µFTIR-based riverine studies. No additional data correction is warranted at this time; the key outstanding methodological uncertainty is the µFTIR objective used, which affects absolute concentrations but not the relative risk ranking.

4.2.1.3 4.2.1.3 Comparative apsd values: this study vs. literature

4.2.2 4.2.2 Fit C-PSD model to Particle Surface Area

cpsd_fit_area_fragment <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(area_um2), bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 50000)),  list(shape = "fragment"))
cpsd_fit_area_fiber    <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(area_um2), bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000)), list(shape = "fiber"))
cpsd_fit_area          <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::pull(area_um2),              bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000)),                          list(shape = "all"))

cat("Fragment Surface Area: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fragment$a_cpsd, 2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fragment$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fragment$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fragment$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm²\n")
## Fragment Surface Area: alpha = -1.7 +- 0.023 , LOD = 9500 – 48000 µm²
cat("Fiber Surface Area:    alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fiber$a_cpsd,    2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fiber$se_a_cpsd,    2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fiber$lower_lod_used_um,    2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_area_fiber$upper_lod_um,    2), "µm²\n")
## Fiber Surface Area:    alpha = -0.98 +- 0.012 , LOD = 9500 – 60000 µm²
cat("All Shape Surface Area: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_area$a_cpsd,         2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_area$se_a_cpsd,         2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_area$lower_lod_used_um,          2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_area$upper_lod_um,          2), "µm²\n")
## All Shape Surface Area: alpha = -1.3 +- 0.012 , LOD = 10000 – 52000 µm²

For reference, Kooi et al. (2021) found the following: * Freshwater surface area: alpha = 2.00 +- 0.065; lower LOD = 482,000 um^2 * Marine surface water: alpha = 1.50 +- 0.009; lower LOD = 2,380 um^2

  # film  = cpsd_fit_film,

4.2.3 Volume C-PSD Fitting

volume_particle() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) converts length LODs to volume LODs using the same shape-dependent geometry as the particle volume calculation in section 3.1.1.

# Translate length LODs to volume LODs using shape geometry
fragment_volume_lod_lower <- volume_particle("fragment", cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_um, cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_um, cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_um)
fragment_volume_lod_upper <- volume_particle("fragment", cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um, cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um, cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um)
fiber_volume_lod_lower    <- volume_particle("fiber",    cpsd_fit_fiber$lower_lod_um, cpsd_fit_fiber$lower_lod_um, cpsd_fit_fiber$lower_lod_um)
fiber_volume_lod_upper    <- volume_particle("fiber",    cpsd_fit_fiber$upper_lod_um, cpsd_fit_fiber$upper_lod_um, cpsd_fit_fiber$upper_lod_um)
cat("Fragment volume LOD: [", signif(fragment_volume_lod_lower, 2), ",", signif(fragment_volume_lod_upper, 2), "] µm³\n")
## Fragment volume LOD: [ 450000 , 2.2e+07 ] µm³
cat("Fiber    volume LOD: [", signif(fiber_volume_lod_lower,    2), ",", signif(fiber_volume_lod_upper,    2), "] µm³\n")
## Fiber    volume LOD: [ 4200000 , 8.7e+07 ] µm³
cpsd_fit_volume_fragment <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(V_um3), bin_um = 1e3, fit_range_um = c(fragment_volume_lod_lower, fragment_volume_lod_upper)), list(shape = "fragment"))
cpsd_fit_volume_fiber    <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(V_um3), bin_um = 1e4, fit_range_um = c(fiber_volume_lod_lower,    fiber_volume_lod_upper)),    list(shape = "fiber"))
cpsd_fit_volume          <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_river |> dplyr::pull(V_um3),                                       bin_um = 1e2, fit_range_um = c(1e7, 1e8)),                                             list(shape = "all"))

cat("Fragment Volume: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fragment$a_cpsd, 2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fragment$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fragment$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fragment$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm³\n")
## Fragment Volume: alpha = -1.5 +- 0.0086 , LOD = 870000 – 2e+06 µm³
cat("Fiber Volume:    alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fiber$a_cpsd,    2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fiber$se_a_cpsd,    2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fiber$lower_lod_used_um,    2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_fiber$upper_lod_um,    2), "µm³\n")
## Fiber Volume:    alpha = -0.88 +- 0.01 , LOD = 9400000 – 1.9e+07 µm³
cat("All Shape Volume: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume$a_cpsd,         2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_volume$se_a_cpsd,         2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume$lower_lod_used_um,          2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_volume$upper_lod_um,          2), "µm³\n")

4.2.4 4.2.4 Per-river C-PSD fits (length, surface area, and volume — faceted)

# Fit C-PSD per river × shape for all three metrics.
# Uses tryCatch to handle sparse data combinations gracefully.
safe_cpsd <- function(data, ...) {
  if (length(data) < 10) return(list(valid = FALSE))
  tryCatch(
    c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(data, ...), list(valid = TRUE)),
    error = function(e) list(valid = FALSE)
  )
}

cpsd_loc_shape_length <- lapply(setNames(locations, locations), function(loc) {
  sub <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc)
  list(
    fragment = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5),
    fiber    = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5),
    all      = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5)
  )
})

cpsd_loc_shape_area <- lapply(setNames(locations, locations), function(loc) {
  sub <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc)
  list(
    fragment = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(area_um2),
                         bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 50000)),
    fiber    = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(area_um2),
                         bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000)),
    all      = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::pull(area_um2),
                         bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000))
  )
})

cpsd_loc_shape_vol <- lapply(setNames(locations, locations), function(loc) {
  sub <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc)
  list(
    fragment = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(V_um3),
                         bin_um = 1e3, fit_range_um = c(fragment_volume_lod_lower, fragment_volume_lod_upper)),
    fiber    = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(V_um3),
                         bin_um = 1e4, fit_range_um = c(fiber_volume_lod_lower, fiber_volume_lod_upper)),
    all      = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::pull(V_um3),
                         bin_um = 1e2, fit_range_um = c(1e7, 1e8))
  )
})

# Helper: extract LOD bounds from a fit object
.lod_bounds <- function(fo) {
  lod_lo <- if (!is.null(fo$lower_lod_used_um) && is.finite(fo$lower_lod_used_um))
               fo$lower_lod_used_um else fo$lower_lod_um
  list(lo = lod_lo, hi = fo$upper_lod_um)
}

# Extract predicted lines + 95% CI ribbon within each fit's valid LOD window
extract_fit_lines <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc[[loc]]), function(shp) {
      fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][[shp]]
      if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$fit)) return(NULL)
      b <- .lod_bounds(fo)
      if (!is.finite(b$lo) || !is.finite(b$hi) || b$lo >= b$hi) return(NULL)
      grid <- tibble::tibble(L_low = seq(b$lo, b$hi, length.out = 80))
      pred <- tryCatch(predict(fo$fit, newdata = grid, se.fit = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
      if (is.null(pred)) return(NULL)
      tibble::tibble(metric = metric_name, shape = shp, location = loc,
                     L_low    = grid$L_low,
                     logN_fit = pred$fit,
                     logN_lo  = pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit,
                     logN_hi  = pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
    }))
  }))
}

# Extract raw binned data points with an in_lod flag for opacity mapping
extract_fit_points <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc[[loc]]), function(shp) {
      fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][[shp]]
      if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$bins)) return(NULL)
      b <- .lod_bounds(fo)
      fo$bins |>
        dplyr::arrange(L_low) |>
        dplyr::mutate(
          N_ge   = rev(cumsum(rev(n))),
          in_lod = is.finite(b$lo) & is.finite(b$hi) & L_low >= b$lo & L_high <= b$hi
        ) |>
        dplyr::filter(L_low > 0, N_ge > 0) |>
        dplyr::transmute(metric = metric_name, shape = shp, location = loc,
                         L_low, logN = log10(N_ge), in_lod)
    }))
  }))
}

# River location colour palette (defined once, reused in both chunks)

4.2.5 4.2.5 Per-river power-law slopes across size metrics

The per-location C-PSD fits from Section 4.2.4 yield a BN-PSD slope apsd for each combination of river location and size metric (length, surface area, volume). Comparing these slopes across metrics shows how the shape of the size distribution changes with the geometric measure used, and whether location-to-location variation is consistent across metrics.

# Extract per-location a_psd for surface area and volume from the per-river fits
extract_loc_slopes <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][["all"]]
    if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$fit)) return(NULL)
    tibble::tibble(location = loc, a_psd = fo$a_psd, se_a_cpsd = fo$se_a_cpsd, metric = metric_name)
  }))
}

loc_slopes_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(loc_summary, location, a_psd, se_a_cpsd, metric = "Length (µm)"),
  extract_loc_slopes(cpsd_loc_shape_area, "Surface Area (µm²)"),
  extract_loc_slopes(cpsd_loc_shape_vol,  "Volume (µm³)")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric   = factor(metric, levels = c("Length (µm)", "Surface Area (µm²)", "Volume (µm³)")),
    location = factor(location, levels = locations)
  )

# Reference slopes (Segur 2026 ocean mean, length metric)
ref_slopes <- data.frame(
  metric    = factor("Length (µm)", levels = levels(loc_slopes_all$metric)),
  ref_slope = -2.66,
  ref_label = "Segur 2026\nfragment mean"
)

ggplot2::ggplot(loc_slopes_all,
    ggplot2::aes(x = location, y = a_psd, color = location)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(
    data = ref_slopes,
    ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ref_slope),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_psd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_psd + se_a_cpsd),
    width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = loc_palette, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "River location",
    y        = expression(italic(a)[psd] ~ "=" ~ italic(a)[cpsd] - 1),
    title    = "BN-PSD slope by river location and size metric",
    subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE  |  Dashed = Segur 2026 fragment reference (length only)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
    strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")
  )

Following the probabilistic rescaling approach (e.g., Coffin et al. 2022), treat alpha as uncertain and represent it by a distribution (commonly normal, truncated to plausible bounds).

The fitted C-PSD slope is treated as uncertain (normal distribution truncated to [−6, −1.1]) to propagate slope uncertainty through subsequent rescaling and risk characterization. alpha_dist() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.

alpha    <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd, sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_cpsd, n = n_mc)
alpha_mu <- mean(alpha)
alpha_se <- sd(alpha)
summary(alpha)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##  -2.042  -1.947  -1.925  -1.925  -1.904  -1.813

The resulting alpha distribution has mean -1.925 and SD 0.031.

4.3 4.4 Length-to-width ratio distribution

Particle width-to-length ratios (W/L = 1/aspect_ratio) are bootstrapped to propagate shape uncertainty into the PSSDplusplus particle alignment model. bootstrap_aspect_ratio() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.

raw_particles_river |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = 1 / aspect_ratio, fill = shape)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Width : Length ratio (W/L)", y = "Count",
                title = "Distribution of particle width-to-length ratios by shape") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 15)

R.ave_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_river$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_vals   <- R.ave_result$vals
R.ave_mean   <- R.ave_result$boot_mean
R.ave_sd     <- R.ave_result$boot_sd
print(R.ave_result$summary)
## # A tibble: 1 × 7
##     p05   p50   p95  mean    sd boot_mean boot_sd
##   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1  0.25 0.495 0.668 0.457 0.117     0.457 0.00355

5 5. Step 2 — Rescale measured concentrations to a common size range

5.1 5.1 Power-law integration for rescaling factors

If the differential PSD follows dN/dL = k·L^a, the concentration in [L₁, L₂] is proportional to k/(a+1)·(L₂^(a+1) − L₁^(a+1)) (a ≠ −1). The rescaling correction factor is:

CF = N(L_target_min, L_target_max) / N(L_meas_min, L_meas_max)

correction_factor() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R (Coffin et al. 2022). The measured size range is bias-corrected using the C-PSD LOD window from cpsd_fit_all.

# Align monitoring LOD window to the C-PSD detection limits
monitoring <- monitoring |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Lmin_biascorr_um = pmax(Lmin_measured_um, cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_um, na.rm = TRUE),
    Lmax_biascorr_um = pmin(Lmax_measured_um, cpsd_fit_all$upper_lod_um,  na.rm = TRUE)
  )

L_meas_min_use <- median(monitoring$Lmin_biascorr_um, na.rm = TRUE)
L_meas_max_use <- median(monitoring$Lmax_biascorr_um, na.rm = TRUE)

# Convert measured range to target range [1, 5000] µm, propagating alpha uncertainty
cf_rescale <- correction_factor(
  a          = alpha,
  L_meas_min = L_meas_min_use,
  L_meas_max = L_meas_max_use,
  L_tar_min  = 1,
  L_tar_max  = 5000
)

quantile(cf_rescale, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
##       5%      50%      95% 
## 165.8364 207.3078 260.4761

The median rescaling factor is 207.31 (90% CI: 165.84 – 260.48), applied to convert concentrations measured over 165 – 385 µm to the target range of 1 – 5000 µm.

5.2 5.2 Optional additional bias terms as probability distributions

Coffin et al. (2022) describe two additional multiplicative correction terms that can be composed with the power-law rescaling CF:

  • Fiber correction factor (\(\text{CF}_\text{fiber}\)): Accounts for systematic fiber under-retention during mesh-based sampling (net trawls, pump filtration with woven sieves). In those contexts, the slender geometry of fibers allows them to pass through mesh apertures lengthwise, producing under-counts that are proportional to mesh size (Zhao et al. 2026). A log-normal distribution is appropriate because the factor is right-skewed and strictly positive.
  • Plastic proportion factor (\(p_\text{plastic}\)): The fraction of detected particles confirmed as plastic by spectroscopy. A Beta(\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) distribution is appropriate because the factor is bounded to [0, 1].

Assessment for this dataset. A fiber correction factor is not applied here for two reasons:

  1. Sampling method: The present monitoring data are from µFTIR analysis of membrane-filtered whole-water grab samples (pump collection), not mesh net trawls. Zhao et al. (2026) demonstrate that the dramatic fiber under-capture they quantify (0.7% efficiency at 330 µm mesh) arises specifically from the geometric interaction of elongated particles with woven mesh apertures. Membrane pore filtration retains particles primarily by size, so this mechanism does not apply.
  2. Power-law extrapolation already corrects for sub-LOD fibers: The correction_factor() function in Step 2 uses the fitted power-law slope to integrate particle counts from the measured size range (50–500 µm) to the target range (1–5000 µm). This extrapolation already accounts for undetected small fibers in a self-consistent way. Applying an additional fiber CF on top would double-count this adjustment.

The fiber slope (\(a_\text{psd}\) = -2.69) is shallower than the fragment slope (-3.71), which may reflect residual under-retention of the finest fibers through nominal 50 µm filter pores, but this cannot be corrected without fiber-specific filter efficiency data. See Section 4.2.1.2 for the literature comparison.

# Optional multiplicative factors — not applied for this µFTIR membrane-filter dataset.
# Retain code for reference and potential future use with mesh-sampled datasets.
fiber_cf   <- rlnorm(n_mc, meanlog = log(2.0), sdlog = 0.5)    # illustrative; not applied
plastic_pf <- pmin(rbeta(n_mc, shape1 = 20, shape2 = 3), 1.0)  # illustrative; not applied

combined_cf <- cf_rescale  # fiber_cf and plastic_pf not multiplied in: see rationale above
quantile(combined_cf, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
##       5%      50%      95% 
## 165.8364 207.3078 260.4761

5.3 5.3 Apply probabilistic correction to monitoring data

We treat each monitoring sample’s corrected concentration as:

C_corrected = C_measured * combined_cf_draw, with combined_cf_draw sampled in Monte Carlo.

This yields a distribution per monitoring sample, and a pooled exposure distribution across samples.

# For simplicity, assume the same CF distribution applies to each sample.
# If CF depends on site/method/shape, build CF distributions per strata and apply accordingly.

C_corrected_draws <- monitoring |>
  mutate(idx = row_number()) |>
  tidyr::crossing(draw = 1:3000) |>
  mutate(
    cf = sample(combined_cf, size = n(), replace = TRUE),
    C_corrected_pL = C_measured_pL * cf
  )

C_corrected_draws |>
  summarise(p05 = quantile(C_corrected_pL, 0.05),
            p50 = quantile(C_corrected_pL, 0.50),
            p95 = quantile(C_corrected_pL, 0.95))

6 6. Step 3 — Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED) via empirical bootstrap

Because environmental monitoring data are typically sparse and highly skewed, a nonparametric bootstrap is often a strong default:

  • Resample (with replacement) the corrected sample-level concentrations.
  • Compute the empirical CDF and desired percentiles per bootstrap replicate.
  • This avoids heavy reliance on a parametric distribution family selection for EEDs.
# Collapse each sample to its median corrected concentration, then bootstrap across samples.
# This isolates site-level variability from correction-factor uncertainty (handled in MC2D below).
# bootstrap_eed() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
C_sample_median <- C_corrected_draws |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(C_corr_med = median(C_corrected_pL), .groups = "drop")

eed_boot <- bootstrap_eed(C_sample_median$C_corr_med, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
summary(eed_boot)
##       q50             q95       
##  Min.   :4.125   Min.   :14.85  
##  1st Qu.:5.226   1st Qu.:27.36  
##  Median :5.413   Median :37.18  
##  Mean   :5.556   Mean   :34.06  
##  3rd Qu.:5.970   3rd Qu.:41.63  
##  Max.   :7.907   Max.   :71.35

The median EED 50th percentile across 100 bootstrap replicates is 5.41 particles/L (90th percentile bootstrap: 37.18 particles/L).

eed_boot_long <- eed_boot |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "stat", values_to = "value") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    stat_label = dplyr::case_when(
      stat == "q50" ~ "EED 50th percentile",
      stat == "q95" ~ "EED 95th percentile",
      TRUE          ~ stat
    )
  )

eed_boot_long |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = value, fill = stat_label, color = stat_label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.75, linewidth = 0.2) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~stat_label, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values  = c("EED 50th percentile" = "#56B4E9",
                                         "EED 95th percentile" = "#E69F00")) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("EED 50th percentile" = "#2A7FAD",
                                         "EED 95th percentile" = "#BF7A00")) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "Corrected concentration (particles/L)",
    y        = "Bootstrap replicates",
    title    = "Bootstrap uncertainty in Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED) percentiles",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "n = ", n_boot, " bootstrap replicates of site-level median corrected concentrations"
    ),
    caption  = "Correction factor (CF) propagated via Monte Carlo; each replicate resamples sites with replacement."
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    strip.text       = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.border     = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
    plot.caption     = ggplot2::element_text(size = 9, color = "gray50", hjust = 0)
  )

7 7. Step 4 — Bespoke hazard thresholds using pSSD++ (ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk)

7.1 7.1 Toxicity dataset

Start with aligned toxicity records for freshwater species (i.e., quality-screened ToMEx 2.0 records aligned to both food dilution and tissue-translocation ERMs using bioaccessibility models and particle traits).

# filter species by environment
tox_data <- tomex2 |> 
   dplyr::filter(
    env_f == "Freshwater",
    Group != "Bacterium", # Drop studies with Bacterium group
    Group != "Plant", # Drop studies with Plant group
    effect.metric != "HONEC", # Drop studies with HONEC effect metric
    tier_zero_tech_f == "Red Criteria Passed", #minimum QC for technical criteria
    tier_zero_risk_f == "Red Criteria Passed", #minimum QC for risk criteria
    risk.13 != 0 #Drop studies that received a score of 0 for endpoints criteria (this also drops studies that have not yet been)
  )

# summarize by group, species, and polymer type to understand tox data included in model
tox_data |> 
  group_by(Group, Species, poly_f, shape_f) |> 
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")
# replace the default parameter matrix distribution with values derived using the C-PSD method here
param_values <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values |> 
  # update parameters from C-PSD method
  mutate(alpha.freshwater = -alpha_mu, # use cPSD - 1 since dN/dL = k * L^a
         alpha.freshwater.sd = alpha_se,
         # additional values need updating:
         ### Length to width ratio
         R.ave.water.freshwater = R.ave_mean,
         R.ave.water.freshwater.sd = R.ave_sd,

         ### polymer density
         #p.ave.freshwater = ,
         #p.ave.freshwater.sd = ,

         ### volume
         a.v.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_volume$a_cpsd, 
         a.v.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_volume$se_a_cpsd,

         ### mass
         #a.m.freshwater = ,
         #a.m.freshwater.sd = ,

         ### surface area
         a.sa.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_area$a_cpsd,# derived value for all shapes
         a.sa.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_area$se_a_cpsd
         )

# generate parameter matrix using bespoke environmental parameter values
param_matrix <- matrix_function(
  n = n_boot, #size of matrix (10,000 is recommended)
  params = param_values, #parameter distribution values 
  #params = PSSDplusplus::param_default_values, #beta-test with defaults
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500, # maximum particle size (microns) to truncate tissue tranlocation size limit distribution to based on biological plausibility
  x1M_set = 1, #minimum particle size to generate distributions to in microns
  x2D_set = 5000 #maximum particle size to generate distributions to in microns
) |> 
  # replace R.ave.water.freshwater with bootstrapped values
   mutate(R.ave.water.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE),
          H_W_ratio.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE)) #H_W ratio is assumed same as length-width ratio

# visualize parameter distributions
param_plots <- parameter_histograms_function(param_matrix) # generate parameter distribution plots
#visualize plots
param_plots$alpha_combined_plot # distribution of alpha parameters

7.2 7.3 Run Monte-Carlo Simulation on Toxicity Data using Parameter Matrix

MC_sim_align_parallel() is the core PSSDplusplus function that aligns each toxicological endpoint to the particle trait distributions defined in param_matrix. For each Monte Carlo replicate (\(i = 1, \ldots, n_\text{sim}\)) it:

  1. Draws a particle trait vector from param_matrix: particle size (\(L\), log-normal), aspect ratio (\(AR\)), density (\(\rho\)), and C-PSD slope (\(\alpha_\text{cpsd}\)).
  2. Applies the bioaccessibility model for each ERM:
    • Food Dilution — computes the volumetric food dilution dose (particles/L) using the particle volume and the organism’s gut volume, converting the reported NOEC/EC dose to an environmentally comparable particle concentration.
    • Tissue Translocation — computes the particle flux to tissue using the size-dependent translocation model; only particles below the translocation size threshold (500 µm) are included.
  3. Aligns each species’ EC dose to a common concentration unit (particles/L equivalent), enabling a multi-species SSD to be constructed from studies that used different MP sizes, shapes, and concentrations.

The output MC_sim_df is a long data frame with one row per toxicological endpoint per Monte Carlo replicate, with columns for the aligned dose (particles_L_food_dilution, particles_L_ox_stress), bioaccessibility group (ingestible, translocatable), and quality tier (risk.13, bio_f). It is then split by ERM and filtered to the relevant endpoints before SSD fitting in Section 7.4.

MC_sim_df <- MC_sim_align_parallel(
  tox_data = tox_data, # toxicity data (ToMEx 2.0 is default)
  param_matrix = param_matrix, # parameter matrix generated in prior cell
  n_sim = n_boot, # size of parameter matrix (ensure this is the same as the size of the matrix generated)
  x1D_set = 1, # minimum particle size to generate distributions to (in microns)
  x2D_set = 5000, # maximum particle size to generate distributions to (in microns)
  num_cores = parallel::detectCores() - 2 # number of cores to use for parallel processing (auto-detect - 2)
)

Split aligned data into ERM- and environment-specific subsets

results_df_food <- dplyr::filter(
  MC_sim_df,
  ingestible != "not ingestible",
  particles_L_food_dilution > 0,
  Group != "Algae"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dose_new_particles_L = particles_L_food_dilution) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(particles_L_food_dilution)
results_df_food_t3_t4 <- dplyr::filter(
  results_df_food,
  risk.13 != 1,
  bio_f %in% c("Organism", "Population")
)

results_df_tissue <- dplyr::filter(
  MC_sim_df,
  translocatable != "not translocatable",
  particles_L_ox_stress > 0
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dose_new_particles_L = particles_L_ox_stress) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(particles_L_ox_stress)
results_df_tissue_t3_t4 <- dplyr::filter(
  results_df_tissue,
  risk.13 != 1,
  bio_f %in% c("Organism", "Population")
)

erm_registry <- list(
  "Food Dilution" = list(base = results_df_food, t3_t4 = results_df_food_t3_t4),
  "Tissue Translocation" = list(base = results_df_tissue, t3_t4 = results_df_tissue_t3_t4)
)

7.3 7.4 Fit pSSD++ distributions for each ERM/environment

# make all pSSDs
pSSDs <- make_all_pSSDs(
  MC_sim_df = MC_sim_df, # ensure aligned data is included
  environments = c("Freshwater"), #specify which environments to include
  erm_registry = erm_registry,
  sim = 30, # specify the number of simulations to run (300 used in publication)
  cv_uf = 0.5, # specify the coefficient of variation for uncertainty factors (acute -> chronic and LOEC/EC50 -> NOEC)
  rmore_method = "lognormal", # method to handle pSSD distribution building (options = 'step' i.e., original trapezoidal method in Wigger et al., 2020, or 'lognormal' - shortcut developed in Coffin et al. (2025))
  parallel = TRUE, #whether or not to use parallel processing
  workers = parallel::detectCores() - 2, # number of worker processes to use for parallel processing
  base_cache_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "pssd_cache"), # directory to store cached pSSD objects (important when running high number of simulations to resume if needed)
  base_output_path = file.path(tempdir(), "pssd_figures"), # directory to store output figures
  overwrite_cache = TRUE # whether or not to overwrite cached pSSD objects
)

8 8. Step 5 — Risk characterization using joint distributions (Monte Carlo)

We now combine: - Exposure: bootstrap distribution (e.g., EED 50th percentile) or full empirical sample distribution. - Hazard: pSSD++-derived HC5/HC10 distributions for each ERM.

A common probabilistic risk metric is: - Risk Quotient (RQ): RQ = Exposure / Hazard. - Probability of exceedance: P(RQ > 1).

Below we compute four RQ distributions: [Food dilution, Tissue translocation] x [HC5, HC10].

# draw_rq_mc1d() and summarize_rq() are sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
n_risk     <- 1000
risk_draws <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz, eed_boot$q50, n_risk = n_risk)
risk_summary <- summarize_rq(risk_draws)
risk_summary
ggplot2::ggplot(risk_draws, ggplot2::aes(x = RQ, fill = as.factor(ERM))) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 60) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(HCx ~ ERM, scales = "free_y",
                      labeller = ggplot2::labeller(HCx = function(x) paste0("HC", x))) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Risk Quotient (Exposure / Hazard) [log10 scale]", y = "count",
                title = "Monte Carlo risk quotient distributions by ERM and HCx") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

The 1D Monte Carlo risk characterization indicates a median RQ of 851.38 for the Food Dilution ERM (HC5; P(RQ>1) = 99.9%) and 0.024 for the Tissue Translocation ERM (HC5; P(RQ>1) = 7.3%). RQ values below 1 indicate exposure concentrations below the hazard threshold for the majority of aquatic species.

10 9. Two-dimensional Monte Carlo (MC2D)

Two-dimensional Monte Carlo (MC2D) to separately handle: - uncertainty (e.g., correction factors, hazard model uncertainty), - variability (true spatial/temporal variability in exposure).

Below, the outer loop samples uncertain parameters (a correction factor draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx), while the inner loop samples exposure variability from the observed monitoring concentrations.

How to read the MC2D outputs

  • Each outer iteration represents one plausible “world” of uncertainty (sampling one CF draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx).
  • Within that world, the inner loop samples exposure variability across sites/dates (using the observed measured concentrations).
  • For each outer iteration, we summarize the resulting RQ distribution as P_exceed, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, and RQ_p99.
  • The distribution of these summaries across iterations quantifies uncertainty in risk metrics, while the inner loop represents variability in exposure.
# mc2d_risk() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
# Outer loop: n_uncertainty = 300 CF + hazard draws (uncertainty).
# Inner loop: n_variability = 1000 exposure draws per outer iteration (variability).
mc2d_results <- mc2d_risk(
  monitoring_df = monitoring,
  combined_cf   = combined_cf,
  haz_df        = haz,
  n_uncertainty = 300,
  n_variability = 1000,
  seed          = 1
)

mc2d_summary <- mc2d_results |>
  dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
  summarise(
    P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
    P_exceed_p95 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.95),
    P_exceed_p05 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.05),
    RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50),
    RQ_p95_med = median(RQ_p95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mc2d_summary
# Visualize uncertainty in exceedance probability (outer loop)
mc2d_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = P_exceed, fill = ERM)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  facet_grid(HCx ~ ERM, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(HCx = function(x) paste0("HC", x))) +
  labs(x = "P(RQ > 1) across uncertainty", y = "count",
       title = "MC2D uncertainty distribution for exceedance probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Diagnostic: compare uncertainty spread of P_exceed across ERM/HCx
mc2d_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.factor(HCx), y = P_exceed, fill = ERM)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) paste0("HC", x)) +
  labs(x = "HCx", y = "P(RQ > 1)",
       title = "MC2D uncertainty spread in exceedance probability") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)

# Diagnostic: CF influence on exceedance probability
mc2d_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cf, y = P_exceed, color = ERM)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~HCx, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(HCx = function(x) paste0("HC", x))) +
  labs(x = "Correction factor draw", y = "P(RQ > 1)",
       title = "Relationship between correction factor and exceedance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Diagnostic: distribution of high-end risk (RQ_p95)
mc2d_results |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(RQ_p50, RQ_p95, RQ_p99),
                      names_to = "stat", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = ERM)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  facet_grid(stat ~ HCx, scales = "free",
             labeller = labeller(HCx = function(x) paste0("HC", x))) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Risk Quotient", y = "density",
       title = "MC2D uncertainty distribution for RQ summaries (log10 scale)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

11 10. Sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analysis to identify dominant uncertainty contributors (e.g., alpha, plastic proportion, analytical recovery).

11.1 10.1 Morris elementary effects (beta test)

The Morris method is a global screening approach. It is efficient for ranking inputs by importance using elementary effects:

  • mu* (mean absolute effect): overall importance
  • sigma: nonlinearity or interactions

Below is a small budget setup for beta testing. It uses param_values to define factor ranges and evaluates the MC2D model output metric RQ_p50. Increase morris_r, morris_levels, and the internal MC sizes for production.

# param_bounds() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
morris_params  <- param_bounds(param_values, k = 2)
morris_subset  <- c("alpha.freshwater", "R.ave.water.freshwater", "a.sa.freshwater")
morris_params  <- if (all(morris_subset %in% morris_params$param)) {
  dplyr::filter(morris_params, param %in% morris_subset)
} else {
  dplyr::slice(morris_params, 1:min(4, nrow(morris_params)))
}
morris_params
# Helper: build hazard distributions from a custom param_values dataframe (small budgets for beta test)
build_haz_from_params <- function(pv = param_values,
                                  n_matrix = 2,
                                  n_sim = 2,
                                  sim = 2,
                                  num_cores = 1) {
  param_matrix_i <- matrix_function(
    n = n_matrix,
    params = pv,
    upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
    x1M_set = 1,
    x2D_set = 5000
  )

  MC_sim_df_i <- MC_sim_align_parallel(
    tox_data = tox_data,
    param_matrix = param_matrix_i,
    n_sim = n_matrix,
    x1D_set = 1,
    x2D_set = 5000
  )

  results_df_food_i <- dplyr::filter(
    MC_sim_df_i,
    ingestible != "not ingestible",
    particles_L_food_dilution > 0,
    Group != "Algae"
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(dose_new_particles_L = particles_L_food_dilution) |>
    tidyr::drop_na(particles_L_food_dilution)
  results_df_food_t3_t4_i <- dplyr::filter(
    results_df_food_i,
    risk.13 != 1,
    bio_f %in% c("Organism", "Population")
  )

  results_df_tissue_i <- dplyr::filter(
    MC_sim_df_i,
    translocatable != "not translocatable",
    particles_L_ox_stress > 0
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(dose_new_particles_L = particles_L_ox_stress) |>
    tidyr::drop_na(particles_L_ox_stress)
  results_df_tissue_t3_t4_i <- dplyr::filter(
    results_df_tissue_i,
    risk.13 != 1,
    bio_f %in% c("Organism", "Population")
  )

  erm_registry_i <- list(
    "Food Dilution" = list(base = results_df_food_i, t3_t4 = results_df_food_t3_t4_i),
    "Tissue Translocation" = list(base = results_df_tissue_i, t3_t4 = results_df_tissue_t3_t4_i)
  )

  pSSDs_i <- make_all_pSSDs(
    MC_sim_df = MC_sim_df_i,
    environments = c("Freshwater"),
    erm_registry = erm_registry_i,
    sim = sim,
    cv_uf = 0.5,
    rmore_method = "lognormal",    
    parallel = T,
    workers = parallel::detectCores() - 1,
    base_cache_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "morris_pssd_cache"),
    base_output_path = file.path(tempdir(), "morris_pssd_figures"),
    overwrite_cache = TRUE
  )

  haz_HC5_food_i <- pSSDs_i$`Tier3_Freshwater_Food Dilution`$summary_05$df |>
    mutate(HCx = 5, ERM = "Food Dilution")
  haz_HC10_food_i <- pSSDs_i$`Tier3_Freshwater_Food Dilution`$summary_10$df |>
    mutate(HCx = 10, ERM = "Food Dilution")
  haz_HC5_tissue_i <- pSSDs_i$`Tier3_Freshwater_Tissue Translocation`$summary_05$df |>
    mutate(HCx = 5, ERM = "Tissue Translocation")
  haz_HC10_tissue_i <- pSSDs_i$`Tier3_Freshwater_Tissue Translocation`$summary_10$df |>
    mutate(HCx = 10, ERM = "Tissue Translocation")

  bind_rows(haz_HC5_food_i, haz_HC10_food_i, haz_HC5_tissue_i, haz_HC10_tissue_i)
}
# Morris model: returns a scalar RQ_p50 (median across ERM/HCx) for each input set.
# tryCatch handles PSSDplusplus failures at small budget sizes.
morris_model <- function(X) {
  apply(X, 1, function(x_row) {
    pv <- param_values
    for (j in seq_along(x_row)) {
      pv[[colnames(X)[j]]] <- x_row[j]
    }
    tryCatch({
      haz_i  <- build_haz_from_params(pv, n_matrix = 3, n_sim = 3, sim = 15, num_cores = 5)
      mc2d_i <- mc2d_risk(
        monitoring_df = monitoring,
        combined_cf   = combined_cf,
        haz_df        = haz_i,
        n_uncertainty = 50,
        n_variability = 200,
        seed          = 1
      )
      result <- median(mc2d_i$RQ_p50, na.rm = TRUE)
      if (is.nan(result) || is.na(result)) NA_real_ else result
    }, error = function(e) NA_real_)
  })
}

# Small Morris budget for beta test

morris_r      <- 3

  design = list(type = "oat", levels = morris_levels, grid.jump = 1),
  binf   = morris_params$min,
  bsup   = morris_params$max
)

morris_design$y <- morris_model(morris_design$X)

# Defensive extraction: handles NULL, wrong-length, or all-NaN returns from tell()
.pull_morris <- function(x, n) {
  if (is.null(x)) return(rep(NA_real_, n))
  v <- as.numeric(x)
  if (length(v) != n) {
    v <- c(x)
    if (length(v) != n) return(rep(NA_real_, n))
  }
  # Coerce NaN → NA for consistent downstream handling
  v[is.nan(v)] <- NA_real_
  v
}

11.2 10.2 µFTIR objective: critical assessment of the detection floor and its intersection with the LOD/CF workflow

11.2.1 Instrument configuration

The µFTIR analysis used an objective equivalent to ~4× magnification with 25 µm pixel size. At this pixel resolution, the practical minimum detectable particle size (requiring ≥ 2 pixels across the shortest dimension) is approximately 50 µm — consistent with the L_meas_min = 50 µm parameter used throughout this workflow. This value is already embedded in the correction factor (CF) calculation and is not an additional bias to correct.

11.2.2 Why the Wang et al. (2026) ×33 scaling factor does not apply here

Wang et al. (2026) found that a 4× µFTIR objective (20 µm pixel) detects only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to a 25× reference (2 µm pixel). At face value this suggests a ×33 upward scaling should be applied to our concentrations. This is incorrect for the following reasons:

1. The 97% “missed” particles lie almost entirely below our measurement floor.

The 25× objective in Wang et al. detects particles as small as ~4 µm. The 4× objective detects only those ≥ ~40–50 µm. The difference (97% of total particle count) is dominated by particles in the 4–50 µm size class. Our workflow already treats L_meas_min = 50 µm as the lower detection floor and uses the power-law CF to extrapolate particle counts from this floor down to 1 µm. The Wang et al. sub-50 µm particles are not “missing” from our analysis — they are the precise population that the correction_factor() function reconstructs via power-law integration.

2. Within the measured range (50–500 µm), the 4×/25 µm system is effective.

At 25 µm pixel size:

Particle size Pixels across Detection status
50 µm 2 px Marginal (meets minimum)
100 µm 4 px Reliable
200 µm 8 px Well-resolved
500 µm 20 px Fully resolved

For particles at or above 100 µm — which covers the entire Segur LOD fitting window (fragments: 95–350 µm; all shapes: 165–385 µm) — detection is reliable with this pixel size. The ×33 correction factor was derived from total particle counts including the sub-50 µm population; it does not represent within-range inefficiency.

3. The Segur LOD algorithm implicitly handles the marginal 50–100 µm zone.

The Segur LOD search specifically identifies the size window where the C-PSD is most linear (\(R^2 \geq 0.90\)). The 50–100 µm region, where detection by the 4×/25 µm system may be incomplete, would manifest as a deviation from power-law behavior at the lower end of the binned distribution — and would therefore be excluded from the fitting window. Indeed, the fitted lower LODs (95 µm for fragments, 165 µm pooled) are well above 50 µm, confirming that the algorithm already pushed the lower bound into the reliable detection zone.

4. Applying ×33 on top of the existing CF would double-count.

The current CF has a median of 207.3× (90% CI: 165.8–260.5×). This already accounts for the unmeasured sub-50 µm population via power-law extrapolation. Multiplying C_corrected by an additional 33× would apply a second, conflicting correction to the same particle pool, producing a total inflation factor of ~6841× — far in excess of any defensible estimate.

11.2.3 Residual uncertainty: the 50–100 µm marginal zone

The one genuine uncertainty from the 4×/25 µm configuration is incomplete counting in the 50–100 µm particle size class. Particles in this range occupy 2–4 pixels and may be undercounted by approximately 10–30% relative to what a 15× system would detect. The sensitivity analysis below quantifies the effect of adjusting L_meas_min from 50 µm to 100 µm, which effectively removes the marginal zone from the measured concentration estimate and lets the CF extrapolate it instead.

# Compare CF and risk outcomes under two L_meas_min assumptions:
# 50 µm (current, includes marginal zone) vs 100 µm (excludes marginal zone — conservative floor)
lmeas_scenarios <- list(
  "L_meas_min = 50 µm (current)" = list(L_lo = 50,  L_hi = 500),
  "L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative)" = list(L_lo = 100, L_hi = 500)
)

lmeas_cf_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(lmeas_scenarios), function(scen) {
  s   <- lmeas_scenarios[[scen]]
  cf_s <- correction_factor(
    a           = alpha,                  # same alpha draws (n_mc)
    L_meas_min  = s$L_lo,
    L_meas_max  = s$L_hi,
    L_tar_min   = 1,
    L_tar_max   = 5000
  )
  data.frame(
    scenario = scen,
    CF_p05   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.05),  1),
    CF_med   = round(median(cf_s),           1),
    CF_p95   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.95),  1)
  )
}))

knitr::kable(lmeas_cf_summary,
  caption = paste0(
    "Correction factor (50–500 µm → 1–5000 µm) under alternative lower detection limits. ",
    "Using α_cpsd = ", round(cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd, 3), " (all shapes, Segur LOD). ",
    "n_mc = ", n_mc, " Monte Carlo draws."
  ),
  col.names = c("Scenario", "CF 5th pct", "CF median", "CF 95th pct")
)
Correction factor (50–500 µm → 1–5000 µm) under alternative lower detection limits. Using α_cpsd = -1.926 (all shapes, Segur LOD). n_mc = 20000 Monte Carlo draws.
Scenario CF 5th pct CF median CF 95th pct
5%…1 L_meas_min = 50 µm (current) 35.3 42.4 51.1
5%…2 L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative) 74.2 91.5 113.5

Raising L_meas_min from 50 to 100 µm increases the median CF from 42.4× to 91.5× — a modest change that reflects the additional particles in the 50–100 µm range being moved from “measured” to “extrapolated.” This is the appropriate sensitivity analysis for this instrument configuration: it brackets the range of outcomes depending on whether the marginal detection zone is treated as reliably measured or excluded and reconstructed via power-law. The current workflow (L_meas_min = 50 µm) is the less conservative (lower CF) choice; if the 50–100 µm counts are systematically low due to detection limits, the true concentration may be closer to the L_meas_min = 100 µm estimate.

Summary. No additional objective-based correction factor is applied to C_measured_pL. The existing workflow already accounts for instrument detection limits through (1) the L_meas_min = 50 µm floor that reflects the 4×/25 µm pixel detection limit, and (2) the power-law CF that extrapolates particle counts from this floor to the 1 µm target. The Segur LOD fitting window (≥ 165 µm) lies entirely within the reliable detection zone of the instrument. The Wang et al. (2026) ×33 factor would be appropriate only if converting a 4× total particle count to an equivalent 25× total count without any power-law extrapolation — not in combination with the CF approach used here.

12 11. Sediment — Beach Sand

12.1 11.1 Derive power-law values from raw sediment particle data

# import sediment particle data (beach sand as sediment proxy)
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles |> 
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "beach sand")

# ---- Thickness (height) factor from sediment data ----
ratio_tbl_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1 / aspect_ratio,
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ---- Volumes ----
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl_sed |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

12.1.1 Particle length

cpsd_fit_sed_frag  <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_sed |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "fragment"))
cpsd_fit_sed_fiber <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_sed |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "fiber"))
cpsd_fit_sed_all   <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_sed |> dplyr::pull(length_um),              bin_um = 5), list(shape = "all"))

alpha_sed <- alpha_dist(
  mu = cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd,
  sd = cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_cpsd,
  n = 20000
)

alpha_sed_mu <- mean(alpha_sed)
alpha_sed_se <- sd(alpha_sed)

cat("Sediment All: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd, 2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm\n")

12.2 11.3 Sediment monitoring concentrations and EED

monitoring_sed <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds") |> 
  filter(
    sample_type == "beach sand",
    material_simple == "plastic",
    sample_or_blank == "sample"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"),
    date = ymd(date_raw),
    sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate,
    # placeholder: update if a sediment-specific concentration column is available
    C_measured_pkg = extrap_conc_PPL,
    Lmin_measured_um = 50,
    Lmax_measured_um = 500
  )

monitoring_sed <- monitoring_sed |>
  mutate(
    Lmin_biascorr_um = pmax(Lmin_measured_um, cpsd_fit_sed_all$lower_lod_um, na.rm = TRUE),
    Lmax_biascorr_um = pmin(Lmax_measured_um, cpsd_fit_sed_all$upper_lod_um, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

L_meas_min_use_sed <- median(monitoring_sed$Lmin_biascorr_um, na.rm = TRUE)
L_meas_max_use_sed <- median(monitoring_sed$Lmax_biascorr_um, na.rm = TRUE)

cf_rescale_sed <- correction_factor(
  a = alpha_sed,
  L_meas_min = L_meas_min_use_sed, 
  L_meas_max = L_meas_max_use_sed,
  L_tar_min  = 1,   
  L_tar_max  = 5000
)

combined_cf_sed <- cf_rescale_sed

C_corrected_draws_sed <- monitoring_sed |>
  mutate(idx = row_number()) |>
  tidyr::crossing(draw = 1:3000) |>
  mutate(
    cf = sample(combined_cf_sed, size = n(), replace = TRUE),
    C_corrected_pkg = C_measured_pkg * cf
  )

C_sample_median_sed <- C_corrected_draws_sed |>
  group_by(sample_id) |>
  summarise(C_corr_med = median(C_corrected_pkg), .groups = "drop")

eed_boot_sed <- bootstrap_eed(C_sample_median_sed$C_corr_med, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
summary(eed_boot_sed)

12.3 11.2 Sediment toxicity data

tox_data_sed <- tomex2 |> 
   dplyr::filter(
    env_f %in% c("Marine", "Freshwater"),
    exposure.route == "sediment",
    Group != "Bacterium",
    effect.metric != "HONEC",
    tier_zero_tech_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    tier_zero_risk_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    risk.13 != 0
  ) |> 
    # since limited data available, and working with estuarine system - combine marine and freshwater species by overwriting environment to be freshwater for all
    mutate(env_f = "Freshwater")

12.3.1 Align Toxicity Data

12.3.1.1 Parameter distributions

R.ave_sed_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_sed$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_sed_vals   <- R.ave_sed_result$vals
R.ave_sed_mean   <- R.ave_sed_result$boot_mean
R.ave_sed_sd     <- R.ave_sed_result$boot_sd

param_values_sed <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values

param_values_sed[[paste0("alpha.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -alpha_sed_mu
param_values_sed[[paste0("alpha.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- alpha_sed_se
param_values_sed[[paste0("R.ave.sediment.freshwater")]] <- R.ave_sed_mean
param_values_sed[[paste0("R.ave.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- R.ave_sed_sd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.v.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.v.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_cpsd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.sa.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_cpsd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.sa.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_area_sed$se_a_cpsd

# pair down to only used parameters
param_values_sed <- param_values_sed |> dplyr::select(contains("sediment.freshwater"), contains("beta"), contains("body"))
param_values_sed

13 12. Ocean Water

Ocean water samples were collected from the coastal/marine environment and analyzed using the same µFTIR workflow as river water. Marine species are evaluated using the PSSDplusplus marine toxicity endpoints and alignment parameters, which characterize exposure and hazard in particles/L rather than particles/kg (sediment).

13.1 12.1 Particle data and C-PSD fitting

13.1.1 Particle volume computation

# Compute W/L thickness ratio from ocean particles (same instrument as river)
ratio_tbl_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(WL = 1 / aspect_ratio) |>
  dplyr::group_by(shape) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::left_join(ratio_tbl_ocean |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = dplyr::case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

cat("Ocean particles: n =", nrow(raw_particles_ocean),
    "| shapes:", paste(sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$shape)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Ocean particles: n = 117 | shapes: fiber, fragment

13.1.2 Particle length

cpsd_fit_ocean_frag  <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "fragment"))
cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "fiber"))
cpsd_fit_ocean_all   <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_ocean |>                                         dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5), list(shape = "all"))

alpha_ocean    <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_cpsd, sd = cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_cpsd, n = n_mc)
alpha_ocean_mu <- mean(alpha_ocean)
alpha_ocean_se <- sd(alpha_ocean)

cat("Ocean All: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_cpsd, 2), "±",
    signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    "| LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–",
    signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm\n")
## Ocean All: alpha = -1.8 ± 0.031 | LOD = 95 – 240 µm

ocean_length_cpsd_plot <- plot_cpsd_multi(ocean_length_fits, title = "Ocean water C-PSD fits by shape", attribute = "Length")

13.1.3 Particle surface area

cpsd_fit_area_ocean_frag  <- c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fragment") |> dplyr::pull(area_um2), bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 50000)),  list(shape = "fragment"))

cat("Ocean All SA: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_cpsd, 2), "±",

13.2 12.2 Ocean monitoring concentrations and EED

monitoring_ocean <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds") |>
  dplyr::filter(
    sample_type    == "ocean water",
    material_simple == "plastic",
    sample_or_blank == "sample"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    date_raw      = stringr::str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"),
    date          = lubridate::ymd(date_raw),
    sample_id     = Client_ID_MSSupdate,
    C_measured_pL = extrap_conc_PPL,
    Lmin_measured_um = 50,
    Lmax_measured_um = 500
  )

cat("Ocean monitoring samples:", nrow(monitoring_ocean), "\n")
## Ocean monitoring samples: 85
monitoring_ocean <- monitoring_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Lmin_biascorr_um = pmax(Lmin_measured_um, cpsd_fit_ocean_all$lower_lod_um, na.rm = TRUE),
    Lmax_biascorr_um = pmin(Lmax_measured_um, cpsd_fit_ocean_all$upper_lod_um,  na.rm = TRUE)
  )

L_meas_min_ocean <- median(monitoring_ocean$Lmin_biascorr_um, na.rm = TRUE)
L_meas_max_ocean <- median(monitoring_ocean$Lmax_biascorr_um, na.rm = TRUE)

cf_rescale_ocean <- correction_factor(
  a          = alpha_ocean,
  L_meas_min = L_meas_min_ocean,
  L_meas_max = L_meas_max_ocean,
  L_tar_min  = 1,
  L_tar_max  = 5000
)
combined_cf_ocean <- cf_rescale_ocean
cat("Ocean CF: median =", round(median(combined_cf_ocean), 1), "× (90% CI",
    round(quantile(combined_cf_ocean, 0.05), 1), "–",
    round(quantile(combined_cf_ocean, 0.95), 1), "×)\n")
## Ocean CF: median = 63.6 × (90% CI 52.8 – 76.9 ×)
C_corrected_draws_ocean <- monitoring_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(idx = dplyr::row_number()) |>
  tidyr::crossing(draw = 1:3000) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cf = sample(combined_cf_ocean, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    C_corrected_pL = C_measured_pL * cf
  )

C_sample_median_ocean <- C_corrected_draws_ocean |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(C_corr_med = median(C_corrected_pL), .groups = "drop")

eed_boot_ocean <- bootstrap_eed(C_sample_median_ocean$C_corr_med, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
summary(eed_boot_ocean)
##       q50              q95       
##  Min.   :0.9525   Min.   :1.461  
##  1st Qu.:1.1303   1st Qu.:2.478  
##  Median :1.4613   Median :2.780  
##  Mean   :1.5279   Mean   :2.567

tox_data_ocean <- tomex2 |>

13.3.1 Parameter distributions

R.ave_ocean_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_ocean$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_ocean_vals   <- R.ave_ocean_result$vals
R.ave_ocean_mean   <- R.ave_ocean_result$boot_mean
R.ave_ocean_sd     <- R.ave_ocean_result$boot_sd

param_values_ocean <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values

param_values_ocean[["alpha.marine"]]          <- -alpha_ocean_mu
param_values_ocean[["alpha.marine.sd"]]       <- alpha_ocean_se
param_values_ocean[["R.ave.water.marine"]]    <- R.ave_ocean_mean
param_values_ocean[["R.ave.water.marine.sd"]] <- R.ave_ocean_sd
param_values_ocean[["a.sa.marine"]]           <- -cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_cpsd
param_values_ocean[["a.sa.marine.sd"]]        <- cpsd_fit_area_ocean$se_a_cpsd
param_values_ocean[["a.v.marine"]]            <- -cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_cpsd
param_values_ocean[["a.v.marine.sd"]]         <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_cpsd
# a.m.marine: use volume slope as proxy (mass ∝ density × volume; constant density → same slope)
param_values_ocean[["a.m.marine"]]            <- -cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_cpsd
param_values_ocean[["a.m.marine.sd"]]         <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_cpsd
# Keep all remaining params from param_default_values (same pattern as river section)
# a.ssa.marine, p.ave.marine etc. retain their validated defaults
param_values_ocean

13.3.2 Build and visualize parameter distributions

param_matrix_ocean <- matrix_function(
  n    = n_boot,
  params = param_values_ocean,
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
  x1M_set = 1,
  x2D_set = 5000,
  include_marine_surface_water     = TRUE,
  include_freshwater_surface_water = FALSE,
  include_marine_sediment          = FALSE,
  include_freshwater_sediment      = FALSE
)

ocean_R_col  <- rlang::sym("R.ave.water.marine")
ocean_HW_col <- rlang::sym("H_W_ratio.water.marine")

param_matrix_ocean <- param_matrix_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    !!ocean_R_col  := sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    !!ocean_HW_col := sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )

tryCatch(
  parameter_histograms_function(param_matrix_ocean, compartments = c("Marine Surface Water"))$alpha_combined_plot,
  error = function(e) message("Parameter histogram skipped: ", conditionMessage(e))
)

pSSDs_ocean <- make_all_pSSDs(
  MC_sim_df    = MC_sim_df_ocean,
  environments = c("Marine"),
  erm_registry = erm_registry_ocean,
  sim          = 30,
  cv_uf        = 0.5,
  rmore_method = "lognormal",

  workers      = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  base_cache_dir   = file.path(tempdir(), "pssd_cache_ocean"),
  base_output_path = file.path(tempdir(), "pssd_figures_ocean"),
  overwrite_cache  = TRUE
)

13.4 12.4 Ocean water probabilistic risk characterization

haz_ocean_HC5_food    <- pSSDs_ocean$`Tier3_Marine_Food Dilution`$summary_05$df        |> dplyr::mutate(HCx = 5,  ERM = "Food Dilution")
haz_ocean_HC10_food   <- pSSDs_ocean$`Tier3_Marine_Food Dilution`$summary_10$df        |> dplyr::mutate(HCx = 10, ERM = "Food Dilution")
haz_ocean_HC5_tissue  <- pSSDs_ocean$`Tier3_Marine_Tissue Translocation`$summary_05$df |> dplyr::mutate(HCx = 5,  ERM = "Tissue Translocation")
haz_ocean_HC10_tissue <- pSSDs_ocean$`Tier3_Marine_Tissue Translocation`$summary_10$df |> dplyr::mutate(HCx = 10, ERM = "Tissue Translocation")

haz_ocean <- dplyr::bind_rows(haz_ocean_HC5_food, haz_ocean_HC10_food, haz_ocean_HC5_tissue, haz_ocean_HC10_tissue)

mc2d_ocean <- mc2d_risk(
  monitoring_df = monitoring_ocean,
  combined_cf   = combined_cf_ocean,
  haz_df        = haz_ocean,
  n_uncertainty = 300,
  n_variability = 1000,
  seed          = 1
)

mc2d_ocean_summary <- mc2d_ocean |>
  dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
    P_exceed_p95 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.95),
    P_exceed_p05 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.05),
    RQ_p50_med   = median(RQ_p50),
    RQ_p95_med   = median(RQ_p95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
mc2d_ocean_summary

13.4.0.1 Visualize ocean risk characterization results

ggplot2::ggplot(mc2d_ocean, ggplot2::aes(x = P_exceed, fill = ERM)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(HCx ~ ERM, scales = "free_y",
                      labeller = ggplot2::labeller(HCx = function(x) paste0("HC", x))) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "P(RQ > 1) across uncertainty", y = "count",
                title = "Ocean water MC2D uncertainty distribution for exceedance probability") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")

Ocean water risk: median P(RQ>1) = 100% (Food Dilution HC5; median RQ = 1.663253^{5}) and 7.9% (Tissue Translocation HC5; median RQ = 0.039).

14 13. Key Findings Summary

C-PSD power-law fits (Segur et al. 2026 algorithm). alpha_cpsd is the C-PSD slope; a_psd = alpha_cpsd − 1 is the differential BN-PSD slope used in PSSDplusplus.
Matrix Shape α_CPSD SE LOD low (µm) LOD high (µm) R²
River water All -1.926 0.031 165 385 0.989
River water Fragment -2.711 0.037 95 350 0.991
River water Fiber -1.692 0.037 175 480 0.972
Sediment All -1.990 0.014 135 560 0.996
Ocean water All -1.767 0.031 95 245 0.991
Ocean water Fragment -2.151 0.043 95 220 0.991
Ocean water Fiber -0.937 0.040 260 770 0.844
